title: Every way to take part
rule: Every fact on this screen names a source in this file. Official means checked on a government, Parliament, regulator or council page; Secondary means a reputable secondary source, labelled as such. Ages and rules differ between the four nations, so every age-related fact says where it applies. Amplify's notes are marked as such.
lede: The political and civic routes open to young people, by age and by nation: registering and voting, standing and serving, getting your view to MPs, peers, committees and government, how laws are made, and taking part in civic life. Where another Amplify screen or the organisation that runs a route already explains it, this screen points there instead of repeating it.

sections.h: What opens up at each age, and where
sections.intro: Choose your nation to see only what applies there. Rules for the whole UK show everywhere.

items.t: Stand or vote for the UK Youth Parliament
items.d: Members of Youth Parliament are 11 to 18. Your route in shows every rung.
You can register from 14, two years before you can vote in Scottish Parliament, Senedd and council elections.

items.t: Start the Duke of Edinburgh's Award
items.d: Any 14 to 24 year old can do their DofE, which includes volunteering.
Under 14 you cannot work for a profit-making organisation even unpaid; charities and community groups set their own age rules.
You can register from 16, two years before you can vote.

items.t: Vote in Scottish Parliament, Senedd and council elections
items.d: 16 and 17 year olds vote in these elections. The UK Parliament voting age is still 18.

items.t: Be a charity trustee of a charitable company or CIO
items.d: The minimum is 16 for a charitable company or charitable incorporated organisation, and 18 for any other charity.
In England and Northern Ireland, 18 is the voting age for every election. The Representation of the People Bill, now in the Lords, would lower the UK Parliament voting age to 16.

items.t: Stand for election as an MP or councillor
items.d: The minimum age to stand for the House of Commons is 18; English council candidates must also be 18 on the day of nomination.
A governor must be 18 or over when elected or appointed, and cannot be a registered pupil at the school.
If you are 18 to 75 and registered to vote, you can be summoned.
Programmes are for 14 to 24 year olds.

sections.note: The Representation of the People Bill, in the House of Lords at committee stage in November 2026, would lower the UK Parliament voting age to 16. Until it becomes law, the ages above stand.

sections.h: Register, then make sure you can vote

items.d: In England, Scotland and Wales it is online. In Northern Ireland, use the paper form from the Electoral Office for Northern Ireland. You register once, not for every election.
A young person's bus pass is not accepted photo ID. If you have no accepted ID, apply for a free Voter Authority Certificate after you have registered.
If you move house or change your name, register again: registration does not follow you.

items.t: Young people are the least likely to be registered
items.d: The Electoral Commission found young people significantly less likely to be correctly registered. Its 2022 data showed 60% of 18 and 19 year olds registered, and 16% of attainers (those old enough to register but not yet to vote).

items.t: Registering at 14 or 16 is the easiest moment
items.d: You can register up to two years before you can vote, so the first election you can vote in finds you already on the register.
The minimum age to stand for the House of Commons is 18.
In England you must be 18 on the day of nomination and have a local connection. Most candidates belong to a party, but you can stand as an independent.
Member of Youth Parliament, youth councils, school councils and the Youth Select Committee are the elected roles open before 18.
In England and Wales, 16 for a charitable company or CIO, 18 for any other charity.
In England a governor must be 18 or over and cannot be a registered pupil at that school.
Funders, regulators and services run youth advisory panels; Anatomy of the state lists them by layer.
In England and Wales anyone 18 to 75 who is registered to vote and has lived in the UK for five years since turning 13 can be called.

sections.h: Get your view to the people who decide

items.d: MPs represent everyone in their area, whether they voted for them or not, so you do not need to be old enough to vote. Write to your own MP only, say what you want them to do, and make it local.
Many MPs hold drop-in surgeries. Mentioning that you are a young person can help.

items.t: Write to a member of the House of Lords
items.d: Peers have no constituencies. Contact one who works on your issue or on a draft law that affects you. Write your own message: bulk mailshots are not accepted.

Committees publish calls for evidence. At Westminster you submit written evidence online; in the Senedd anyone can respond, including by video or audio; the Northern Ireland Assembly welcomes all individuals.

Consultations are generally open to the public and listed on GOV.UK. UK Government consultations have traditionally run for 12 weeks. The Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland governments run their own.
Momentum and Launch window cover petitions: the 10,000 and 100,000 thresholds and how to time one.
Climate Assembly UK was commissioned by six Commons select committees. Its 108 members were chosen by civic lottery to reflect the UK population, and were aged 16 to 79.
People vote directly on how part of a local budget is spent. In Scotland young people can vote in youth budgeting rounds with their Young Scot card.

sections.h: How a Bill becomes law at Westminster

items.d: The Bill's title is read out. There is no debate.
The first debate, on the Bill's main principles, followed by a vote.
Line-by-line scrutiny, where changes (amendments) are debated. It is generally the longest stage.
Also called consideration in the Commons: the whole House considers further amendments.
The final debate on the Bill as amended, usually straight after report stage.
The Bill goes through the same stages in the other House. The two Houses then settle any differences, sometimes going back and forth.
When both Houses agree the text, the Bill is approved by the monarch and becomes an Act of Parliament.

items.t: Private Members' Bills follow the same path
items.d: Bills from backbench MPs go through the same stages as Government Bills.
Issue domains follows the Representation of the People Bill. Inside Parliament explains the Order Paper and the Thursday business statement, which show when each stage is due.
Under 14 you cannot work for a profit-making organisation, even unpaid, and some organisations' insurance does not cover under 16s. Many charities offer roles for 13 to 17 year olds.
For 14 to 24 year olds, with a volunteering section at every level.
Communities & groups lists uniformed groups, youth work and the #iwill movement for youth social action.

The right to peaceful protest is protected by Articles 10 and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, through the Human Rights Act. The police can still put conditions on how and when a protest happens.
Children who protest, in person or online, have human rights that must be respected. If you are taken to a police station, you should have an appropriate adult with you.
Guides exist for England and Wales, for Scotland and for Northern Ireland. Plan with a trusted adult, and read Safeguarding & support first.
Children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, and those views must be given due weight, not just heard.

sections.intro: Dates as published by councils and the Electoral Commission's partners on 17 November 2026. By-elections can be called at any time. This list is rechecked on the monthly content run.

items.d: Councils in many parts of England, and every council in Scotland and Wales, are due to hold elections. In Scotland and Wales you can vote in council elections from 16.

items.t: Northern Ireland Assembly and councils, May 2027
items.d: The next Assembly election is due on or before 6 May 2027, with council elections expected the same month. In Northern Ireland the voting age is 18 for everything.

items.t: Police and crime commissioners, Thursday 4 May 2028
items.d: Also the London Mayor and London Assembly on the same day.

items.t: UK general election, no later than 15 August 2029
items.d: The date is set when Parliament is dissolved. If the Representation of the People Bill becomes law, 16 and 17 year olds would vote in it.

sections.intro: Counted in working days before polling day, so weekends and bank holidays do not count.

items.t: Register: by midnight, 12 working days before
items.d: Miss it and you cannot vote in that election, though your registration still goes through for the next one. The Representation of the People Bill would move the deadline to 5pm on the same day.
New applications to vote by post, in England, Scotland and Wales.

items.t: Voter Authority Certificate: 5pm, 6 working days before
items.d: The free photo ID for voting, if you have no accepted ID. You must be registered first.
Someone you trust votes for you.

sections.intro: Amplify does not support or oppose any party. Members of Youth Parliament campaign without taking sides.

items.t: What a party is, in law
items.d: To put a party name on a ballot paper, the party must be registered with the Electoral Commission, which keeps one register for Great Britain and one for Northern Ireland. Anyone can apply to register a party; the register is public.
Many parties have a youth section with its own age range, often starting in the mid-teens. Each party sets its own rules, so check the party's own pages.
Read each party's manifesto side by side on one issue you care about, rather than taking a summary on trust. The Issue domains screen shows who decides each issue.

sections.h: Voting guides you can read easily

items.t: Easy Read guide to voting and registering
items.d: Made by Mencap for people with a learning disability, their families and supporters, and published on GOV.UK.
See how few young people are registered compared with older people, on Young people in numbers.

sections.h: How a Bill becomes an Act of the Scottish Parliament

items.d: A committee usually takes evidence, then the Parliament debates and decides whether the Bill goes on or is rejected.
Any MSP can propose changes, called amendments.

items.t: Stage 3: final amendments, debate and vote
items.d: The whole Parliament considers further amendments and decides whether to pass the Bill.
A passed Bill is normally sent for Royal Assent after about four weeks and becomes an Act of the Scottish Parliament.

sections.h: How a Bill becomes an Act of the Senedd

items.d: A committee examines the Bill and the Senedd decides whether it should go further.
Every Member can table amendments, but only committee members vote on them at this stage.
All Members consider amendments.
A final debate and vote on the text; with Royal Assent it becomes an Act of the Senedd.

sections.h: How a Bill becomes an Act of the Northern Ireland Assembly

items.d: The Bill is formally introduced and published, with no debate.
A debate on its general principles and a vote on whether it continues.
The relevant committee considers it in detail. This is when you can send or give evidence.
Members debate and vote on amendments on the Assembly floor, then have a final chance to amend.
A final debate and vote on whether to pass the Bill; it then needs Royal Assent to become law.

sections.intro: Every council sets its own rules in its constitution, so the details below are examples: check your own council's website.

items.t: Talk to your ward councillor first
items.d: Your local councillor is often the best first contact for a local issue, and can raise it for you.

items.t: Ask a question at a full council meeting
items.d: Many councils set aside time, often up to 30 minutes, for written questions from people who live or work in the area, submitted days before the meeting.
Councils have their own petition schemes. In some, any councillor can present your petition to a full council meeting for you.

sections.h: Your rights, and who stands up for them

items.d: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have a commissioner for children and young people, and all four report to the UN on how the UK upholds children's rights.

items.t: Scotland made the UN Convention law
items.d: The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 came into force on 16 July 2024, so public bodies in Scotland must respect children's rights in law.

items.t: Get help if your rights are ignored
items.d: The Safeguarding & support screen lists free, confidential helplines.
Citizens UK trains school and college students to listen to their peers and act together on local issues with other community groups.
The National Union of Students brings together more than 600 students' unions representing over 7 million students.
BBC Young Reporter helps 11 to 18 year olds tell their own stories and understand the media; the Student Publication Association supports student newspapers and magazines.
WriteToThem shows everyone who represents you, from councillors to Lords, from your postcode; TheyWorkForYou follows what they say and do in every UK law-making parliament.

The House of Commons offers apprenticeships in most of its teams, advertised at different times of year; most intermediate ones ask for GCSE English and maths at grade 4 or above. The Scottish Parliament runs apprenticeships too. The Civil Service Fast Track Apprenticeship has closed, so check current schemes before you plan around one.
The STEM & tech screen has free routes into coding and data, and Amplify itself is open for contributions.
